extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students and practitioners of classical mechanics and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpt from a mechanics textbook discussing D'Alembert's principle, virtual displacements, conservative vs path-dependent forces, and a philosophical account of the 'economy of science' (theory choice, models, and mathematical aids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include forces due to changing constraints when applying D'Alembert's principle
rubrics_metrics.description: D'Alembert's principle asserts that all the work that can be done in the displacement of a system is done by the impressed forces and not by the connections. But this ceases to be true when the connections undergo changes in time. In this case, the changes of the connections perform work, and we can then apply equation (2) to the displacements that actually take place only provided we add to the impressed forces the forces that produce the changes of the connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constraints depend on time (moving or changing constraints), explicitly include the generalized forces that correspond to the work performed by those changing connections before applying virtual-work/D'Alembert formulations. Failure to include them yields incorrect reduction of equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat acceleration of guiding constraints as equivalent inertial/external effects
rubrics_metrics.description: If a weightless straight line (guide) moves with forced acceleration, a mass free to move on that line behaves as if affected by an additional acceleration (a fictitious/inertial acceleration) on the equivalent fixed line. For example, on a straight line moving upwards with acceleration y, m behaves as if it were affected with a downward acceleration y on the straight line at rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with bodies constrained to accelerate with their guides, incorporate the guide's acceleration as an effective acceleration (or equivalent force) in the relative coordinate equations to obtain the same results as treating the guide as fixed with additional inertial forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate dependent coordinates by time-differentiating constraint equations when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: To get an equation in x alone when x and y are connected by the actual motion (constraint), differentiate the constraint with respect to time and use the resulting relation for substitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A standard procedure for reducing equations of motion: differentiate holonomic constraint relations with respect to time to obtain relations between velocities (and, if needed, accelerations) and substitute to eliminate dependent coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistency by including all forces from the outset
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent differences in modes of treatment arise from a slight inconsistency: for reasons of calculation convenience, not all forces are included at the outset and a portion is left to be dealt with subsequently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For consistent derivations and to avoid conflicting-looking results, include all relevant forces (including constraint forces or driving forces) at the start of the analysis rather than introducing them later as ad-hoc additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply virtual-displacement principles to actual motions only when constraints are time-independent
rubrics_metrics.description: Equation (2) (D'Alembert's principle) refers to instantaneously possible (virtual) displacements. But when the connections of a system are independent of time, the motions that actually take place are 'virtual' displacements, and consequently the principle may be applied to actual motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may replace virtual displacements by actual time displacements in applying D'Alembert if and only if the constraints do not depend on time; otherwise the distinction between virtual and actual displacements matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize conservative (path-independent) forces via potential-function conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: If X, Y, Z are the partial differential coefficients of the same function U (i.e., X = ∂U/∂x, etc.), then the integral of X dx + Y dy + Z dz is a complete differential and the work is a function of coordinates only (path-independent). Otherwise the integral (work) depends on the entire path described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To test whether a force field is conservative (has a force-function/potential), check whether the force components are mutual partial derivatives of one scalar potential. If so, work between endpoints depends only on initial and final coordinates; otherwise compute along the path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand when integrals reduce to single-variable forms (know the motion/path)
rubrics_metrics.description: The integral J (X dx + Y dy + Z dz) can always be found if we can reduce it to a single variable, i.e., if we know the course of the motion in time or the paths which the movable points describe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with non-conservative fields or when no potential exists, explicit knowledge of the path or parametrization of the motion is required to evaluate work integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer economical (concise, general) formulations in science
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the object of science to replace, or save, experiences, by the reproduction and anticipation of facts in thought. The economical office of science is to present facts as concisely as possible so that future cases can be reconstructed mentally rather than re-experienced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate scientific formulations by their ability to reproduce/anticipate many cases with minimal conceptual/mental expenditure; prefer abstractions and symbols that capture the important aspects relevant to practical interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use abstractions and symbols selectively to capture practically important aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: In reproducing facts in thought we never reproduce them in full but only that side which is important to us; our reproductions are invariably abstractions. Language and symbols (numerals, algebraic signs, etc.) are economical contrivances that represent compound sensations at the sacrifice of some precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling, focus on the aspects of phenomena relevant to the intended use; accept necessary abstractions and be explicit about what is omitted or idealized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific ideas must remain anchored to experience and be testable (confirmation/refutation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science must remain in the province of experience but must hasten beyond it, constantly expecting confirmation, constantly expecting the reverse. Where neither confirmation nor refutation is possible, science is not concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat hypotheses as meaningful for science only if they are empirically actionable — capable in principle of being confirmed or refuted by observation/experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value generality: prefer ideas holding across wide domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Those ideas that hold good throughout the widest domains of research and that supplement the greatest amount of experience are the most scientific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing theories or formulations, prefer those that apply more generally (cover more phenomena) while remaining economical and testable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat auxiliary hypotheses and mathematical models as provisional tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Atomic theory and other mental artifices are products devised for the purpose of reproducing groups of facts; the physical inquirer who has Newton's rules will only admit such theories as provisional helps and will strive for a more natural substitute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use models (atoms, higher-dimensional spaces, particular mathematical forms) as pragmatic instruments for explanation and prediction, but avoid reifying them as literal reality unless warranted by experiment; remain open to replacing them with more natural explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value mathematical economy: favor methods that economize calculation and generalize
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics may be defined as the economy of counting. Algebra and the theory of determinants replace repeated numerical operations by symbolic/mechanical procedures so that complex operations need not be recalculated each time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In scientific practice prefer mathematical formulations and algorithms that reduce repetitive labor, allow reuse of prior results, and generalize computations (e.g., algebraic identities, determinants, symbolic manipulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate models with phenomena; decide ontological claims by experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental expedients have nothing whatever to do with the phenomenon itself. Theoretical constructs (e.g., fourth dimension invoked by spiritualists) remain mental fictions until experience provides reason to treat them as more than aids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a clear epistemic separation between model/tool and reality: models are judged first by their explanatory/predictive success and only tentatively ascriptions of 'reality' should follow robust empirical support.
